![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/78735529c93fa6286edc0fdc69d7398ec9cf758f7e46a0fb71702300aadbeb19.png)
Consider the matrix $U$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times2$ matrix $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $U?$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/703a545742438a81183008b90c0336ee51e9fc230d72ed44b02dbd76f0292f7f.png)
e-8413.worked_solution:
Recall that since $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times2$ matrix $A,$ the matrix $U$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

e-8415.knowledge_point: Finding the Columns of the Third Matrix Given Part of a Singular Value Decomposition
e-8415.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/bb8991a8e02d7280b3d24587067ebf0d7e5f5c0518a9f6b1d022e65ed1d42780.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|v_{11}|+|v_{21}|?$
e-8415.worked_solution:
If $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=5$ and $\sigma_2=3.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value $\sigma_1=5.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of $A^T \!A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=25.$ Computing $A^T \! A - 25 I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/be2d743322a536fc213e7e2a00a04c2b902ab15efafedd8a7e6f7935cd5c7592.png)

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T\!A-25I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/1f537b8ae115d1d01a03766d9c2006ca8bbee77e1b99228466642c5e89c0d0ef.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/77be4b42f9c5a8b379de6a74088106b6374bf28c48e9a7ceb2beb55d483afafe.png)

Therefore,

$$
|v_{11}|+|v_{21}| = \left| \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right| + \left| \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right| = \sqrt{2}.
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that since A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of a 2×2 matrix A, the matrix V must be a 2×2 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the norm of the first column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [45−35] has both properties.

after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \,∗\, \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $U$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $U?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that since $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ the matrix $U$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

after.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $m\times n$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m\times m$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n\times n$ matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The matrix $Σ$ must be diagonal but not necessarily orthogonal.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix,the matrix $U$ in the singular value decomposition $UΣ{V}^{T}$ must be orthogonal $4\times 4$ matrix.

- Statement III is false. The matrix $V$ must be orthogonal but not necessarily symmetric.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \,∗\, \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrix $U$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $U?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that since $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ the matrix $U$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
{A}^{T}\,A=[\begin{aligned}68 & 26 \\ 26 & 29\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|?$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$ So, the second column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=16.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-16I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-16I=[\begin{aligned}68 & 26 \\ 26 & 29\end{aligned}]-16[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}52 & 26 \\ 26 & 13\end{aligned}]
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|=|-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}|+|\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}|=\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}.
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=10.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=100.$ 

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 & 42 \\ 42 & 58\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-100I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-100I=[\begin{aligned}58 & 42 \\ 42 & 58\end{aligned}]-100[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-42 & 42 \\ 42 & -42\end{aligned}]
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-100I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|=|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|=\sqrt{2}.
$$

decision.explanation: The second column of V is a unit eigenvector of AᵀA for eigenvalue 3²=9. Subtracting 9I gives the equation 36v₁₂−12v₂₂=0, so v₂₂=3v₁₂. Normalization gives absolute entries 1/√10 and 3/√10, whose sum is 4/√10.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
{A}^{T}\,A=[\begin{aligned}45 & -12 \\ -12 & 13\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|?$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=7$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$ So, the second column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-9I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-9I=[\begin{aligned}45 & -12 \\ -12 & 13\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}36 & -12 \\ -12 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|=|\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}|+|\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}|=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}.
$$
